ta-l1d4q2-d1e97.summary: Transitional paragraph opening the inquiry into divine predication in two articles: whether any predication can be formed about God in a proposition, and whether a person can be predicated of the essence.

ta-l1d4q2-d1e109.summary: First objection that no true proposition predicating something of God can be formed. The truth of a sign consists in its conformity to what it signifies, every predication involves composition, and there is no composition in God.
claims: The truth of a sign is its conformity to the signified, and predication involves composition.

ta-l1d4q2-d1e112.summary: Second objection from Dionysius: in God negations are true and affirmations are 'unfitted' (incompactae). The unfitted is what is not duly ordered, and such disorder introduces falsity into propositions.
claims: Dionysius calls affirmations about God unfitted.

ta-l1d4q2-d1e118.summary: Sed contra. Nothing false can fall under faith, and faith states many affirmative propositions about God, such as that he is three and one.
claims: Faith contains true affirmative propositions about God.

ta-l1d4q2-d1e122.summary: Second sed contra. According to Boethius, no proposition is truer than one in which the same is predicated of itself. In God everything is really the same (possessor and possessed, quod est and quo est), except that one person is not another, so the truest propositions can be formed about God.
claims: Identity statements are the truest propositions, and in God everything is really identical except the persons.

ta-l1d4q2-d1e125.summary: Thomas's determination. Statement follows apprehension, so we must state things as we understand them, and apprehension follows the apprehender's capacity. So our intellect states simple things by way of composition, just as God conversely understands composite things simply. Our intellect forms propositions about God in the manner of the composite things from which it naturally gets its knowledge.
claims: Enunciation follows apprehension, which follows the mode of the knower.
Our intellect forms composite propositions about the simple God, as God knows composite things simply.

ta-l1d4q2-d1e128.summary: Reply to the first objection. As our intellect falls short of knowing the divine majesty, our statements fall short of perfect signification. Still they are true, because the intellect forming them takes two things diverse in mode and the same in reality: it forms subject and predicate according to the diversity of concepts and composes them according to the real identity.
claims: Propositions about God are true because they compose concepts diverse in mode but identical in reality.

ta-l1d4q2-d1e131.summary: Reply to the second objection. Affirmations about God are called 'unfitted' because nothing predicated of him signifies him in the way he is, only in the way our intellect, informed by creatures, grasps him. So predicated names must be understood with their creaturely modes removed. Dionysius teaches that every divine predication is to be read this way: God is wise, and not wise (as others are, with wisdom distinct from the wise), but super-wise, since wisdom is in him more nobly than the name signifies.
claims: Divine names signify according to our mode of understanding, not God's mode of being.
Each name is affirmed, denied in its creaturely mode, and affirmed super-eminently.

ta-l1d4q2-d1e143.summary: First objection that a person cannot be predicated of the essence. A predicate has the character of form, but a person is the supposit of a form or nature.
claims: Predicates function as forms; persons are supposits.

ta-l1d4q2-d1e146.summary: Second objection. A predicate is always signified as inhering in the subject, but a person is not signified as inhering in the essence; rather the reverse.
claims: Predicates are signified as inhering in their subjects.

ta-l1d4q2-d1e149.summary: Third objection. The higher is predicated per se of the lower ('Socrates is a man'), but 'Socrates' is predicated of 'man' only accidentally. The Father is the supposit of the divine nature as Socrates is of human nature, so 'God is the Father' is at most accidentally true.
claims: Predicating a supposit of its nature is accidental predication.
concepts: per se vs. per accidens predication

ta-l1d4q2-d1e153.summary: Fourth objection. 'God' of itself supposits for a person (q. 1, a. 2), and 'one person is Father, Son, and Spirit' is false. So 'one God is Father, Son, and Spirit' is also false.
claims: 'Deus' supposits for a person.

ta-l1d4q2-d1e156.summary: Fifth objection, that 'God is the Trinity' is false. Nothing is predicated of 'man' that is not predicated of some supposit of man, and 'Trinity' is predicated of neither Father, Son, nor Spirit.
claims: Whatever is predicated of a common term is predicated of some of its supposits.

ta-l1d4q2-d1e159.summary: Thomas's determination. In God nature and supposit are wholly indifferent, so there is neither universal nor particular there. As the essence is truly predicated of a person, so a person is truly predicated of the essence. As to mode of signifying, though, a proposition predicating the essence is more proper, since the predicate stands as form.
claims: Because nature and supposit are indifferent in God, person and essence are predicated of each other convertibly.
Predicating the essence of a person is more proper in mode of signifying.

ta-l1d4q2-d1e162.summary: Reply to the first objection. Although a person is a supposit, because supposit and nature are indifferent in God the person is equally simple with the nature, so they are predicated of each other convertibly.
claims: The divine person is equally simple with the nature.

ta-l1d4q2-d1e165.summary: Reply to the second objection, from the same principle: in God possessor and possessed are really the same.
claims: In God the possessor and what is possessed are really identical.

ta-l1d4q2-d1e168.summary: Reply to the third objection. In God there is nothing accidental and no universal and particular, so nothing is said there accidentally or by consequence as in creatures; there are only different modes of signifying.
claims: Nothing is predicated accidentally in God; only modes of signifying differ.

ta-l1d4q2-d1e172.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. 'God' of itself supposits for a person, but indeterminately, not for any person distinctly, and the form it signifies, from which it is imposed, is the common nature, not a personal property. So the unity signified by 'one' refers to the form of divinity, not to the supposit. 'Person' is imposed from personal property as its signified form, so 'one person is Father, Son, and Spirit' is false, since it would signify one personality of three persons.
claims: 'Unus' modifying 'Deus' refers to the common form of divinity.
'One person is Father, Son, and Spirit' is false because 'person' signifies personal property as its form.

ta-l1d4q2-d1e175.summary: Reply to the fifth objection. 'Father', 'Son', and 'Spirit' supposit for distinct persons, but 'God' supposits for a person indeterminately. Because of that indeterminacy, something can be predicated of God that is predicated of none of the distinct persons, just as 'common' or 'species' is said of 'man' but of no individual. Several human persons cannot be predicated together of 'man' because they are not one man, whereas several divine persons are one God and the Trinity. So 'God is three persons' is fitting.
claims: Because 'Deus' supposits indeterminately, 'Trinity' can be predicated of God though not of any single person.
Several divine persons are one God, unlike several human persons.

ta-l1d4q2-d1e184.summary: An expositio textus on Lombard's discussion of 'God the Father begot another himself' (alterum se). Lombard resolves it in two ways. If 'se' is ablative ('another than himself'), the proposition is simply true. If accusative, then either it makes a simple relation, referring to identity of nature, and is true but improper, or it makes a personal relation, referring to the same supposit, and is false. Thomas adds that even on the personal reading it can be true in an emphatic sense ('another like himself'), citing the poet's 'may the gods grant that I not die without me'.
claims: 'Genuit alterum se' is true if 'se' is ablative or makes a simple relation of nature, false if it refers to the same supposit.
An emphatic reading can render it true as 'another like himself'.

ta-l1d4q2-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Question 2 introduces the inquiry into divine predication: whether propositions about God are possible and whether a person can be predicated of the essence.

ta-l1d4q2-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 asks whether true propositions can be formed about God, given that predication involves composition and Dionysius calls affirmations about God 'unfitted'. Against them stand faith's affirmations and Boethius's view that identity predications are truest. Thomas holds that statement follows apprehension, which follows the knower's mode, so we state the simple God compositely. These propositions are true because they compose concepts diverse in mode but identical in reality. They are 'unfitted' only because the names signify according to our creaturely mode, to be affirmed, denied in that mode, and affirmed super-eminently.
claims: True propositions about God are possible; they compose diverse concepts according to real identity.
Divine names are affirmed, denied in their creaturely mode, and affirmed super-eminently.

ta-l1d4q2-Dd1e135.summary: Article 2 asks whether a person can be predicated of the essence ('God is the Father'). Objections argue from predicate as form, from inherence, from the accidental predication of individuals of species, and from 'one God is Father, Son, and Spirit' and 'God is Trinity'. Thomas holds that in God nature and supposit are wholly indifferent, with no universal or particular, so person and essence are predicated of each other convertibly, though predicating the essence is more proper in mode of signifying. 'One God' refers to the common form, while 'one person' would posit one personality. Since 'God' supposits indeterminately, 'Trinity' and 'three persons' are rightly predicated of God.
claims: Person and essence are predicated of each other convertibly, since nature and supposit are indifferent in God.
'God is the Trinity' and 'one God is Father, Son, and Spirit' are true.

ta-l1d4q2-Dd1e179.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 4 analyses Lombard's treatment of 'God the Father begot another himself' (alterum se), distinguishing ablative and accusative readings of 'se' and simple and personal relations, and allowing an emphatic reading.
claims: 'Genuit alterum se' is true on the ablative or simple-relation reading and false on the personal-relation reading.

ta-l1d4q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 4 examines the conditions of true predication about God. Article 1 holds that true propositions about the simple God are possible. Our intellect, knowing from composite creatures, composes concepts that are diverse in mode and identical in reality, and must affirm divine names, deny their creaturely mode, and affirm them super-eminently. Article 2 holds that because nature and supposit are indifferent in God, person and essence are convertibly predicated of each other, so 'God is the Father', 'God is the Trinity', and 'one God is three persons' are true, while 'one person is three' is false. The Expositio analyses the grammar of 'genuit alterum se'.
claims: True propositions about God compose concepts diverse in mode but one in reality.
In God person and essence are convertibly predicated because nature and supposit are indifferent.
'God is the Trinity' is true because 'Deus' supposits indeterminately.
